title: Design HashMap
description: Brute force to optimized: direct addressing versus a fixed bucket array with separate chaining.

blocks.text: Design a HashMap without using any built in hash table library, supporting put(key, value), get(key), and remove(key), where keys and values are non negative integers.

blocks.caption: A hash function compresses keys into buckets; chaining resolves collisions within a bucket

blocks.text: Design a HashMap without using any built in hash table library, supporting put(key, value), get(key), and remove(key), where keys and values are non negative integers.

blocks.title: Analogy: Building Your Own Filing Cabinet From Scratch
blocks.text: Like building a filing system from raw drawers and folders instead of buying a pre made one, where the design choices about how to organize folders directly determine how quickly a specific file can be found later.

blocks.caption: Build the core put, get, and remove operations of a hash map from more basic building blocks

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operation","Result","Why"],"rows":[["put(1, 1)","key 1 now maps to value 1","A brand new key is inserted directly, with no existing entry to overwrite"],["put(2, 2)","key 2 now maps to value 2","Another brand new, independent key-value pair is added"],["get(1)","returns 1","Key 1's stored value is retrieved exactly as it was set"]]}

{"headers":["Operation","Result","Why"],"rows":[["get(3)","key 3 was never set, returns -1","There is no recorded entry for key 3, matching the required not-found behavior"],["put(2, 1)","overwrites key 2's value from 2 to 1","put on an already-existing key updates its value in place rather than creating a duplicate entry"],["get(2)","returns 1","The most recent put's value is what get now returns"]]}

blocks.text: After removing key 2, looking it up again should behave exactly as if it were never set, returning -1.

Before picking any specific data structure, notice what a hash map's three operations actually require: a way to translate an arbitrary key into a location that can be found again quickly, and a way to resolve what happens when two different keys want the same location.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the array were allowed to be as large as the largest possible key, each key could be its own array index directly, guaranteeing O(1) access with zero collisions, but only by paying for every possible key up front, whether or not it is ever actually used.

Observation 2: Since only a limited number of keys are ever really inserted, most of that huge array would sit unused, so the real goal is compressing the enormous key range down into a small, fixed number of buckets.

Observation 3: A simple modulo operation, key mod bucketCount, maps any key into one of a fixed, small number of buckets, but different keys can now land in the same bucket, a collision, purely because of coincidence in their remainders.

Observation 4: Since collisions are rare if bucketCount is reasonably large, each bucket only needs to hold a small list of key-value pairs, checked one by one, which is fast in practice even though it is not a strict O(1) worst case guarantee.

A hash map from scratch is just two decisions: how to compress a huge key space down to a small bucket index, the hash function, and how to handle the occasional collision within one bucket, chaining, a small list per bucket.
This mirrors exactly how production hash maps work internally, just without the automatic bucket-count resizing that keeps chains short as more keys are inserted over time.
Allocate a plain array large enough to directly index by every possible key value, storing each value (or a sentinel for "not present") at the position matching its key.

items: Allocate an array sized to the largest possible key value plus one, initialized to a sentinel meaning "not present".
put(key, value) directly writes value at index key.
get(key) directly reads the value at index key.
remove(key) resets index key back to the sentinel.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The array size, 1,000,001, is chosen to exactly cover every possible key value from the stated constraints, guaranteeing get and put can always index directly without any out-of-bounds risk.
-1 is used as the initial sentinel value throughout the array, exactly matching the required return value for a key that was never set, so get needs no special-case branching at all.
remove(key) simply resets that index back to the sentinel, which is indistinguishable from a key that was never inserted, satisfying the "behaves like never set" requirement directly.

blocks.text: Every operation directly indexes into the array, so correctness is immediate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for every operation.
Space: O(the maximum possible key value), allocated up front regardless of how many keys are actually ever used.

Limitation: allocating an array sized to the entire possible key range wastes enormous amounts of memory whenever only a small number of keys are actually used, which is the exact problem a real hash map is meant to solve.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's O(1) time per operation is already ideal, so nothing needs to speed up algorithmically; the actual problem is the space it pays for something that is barely ever used. Almost the entire allocated array, sized for every conceivable key, sits empty for any realistic sequence of operations, since a typical usage only ever touches a small fraction of the full key range. Shrinking the underlying array down to a small, fixed number of buckets is safe as long as there is a reliable way to still find a given key quickly, which is exactly what a hash function like key mod bucketCount provides: it maps the huge key space down onto a small set of buckets in O(1), and collisions, when they do happen, are resolved by keeping a short list per bucket instead of assuming one slot per key.

Use a fixed, modest number of buckets, and hash each key down to one bucket index using the remainder of dividing by the bucket count. Since different keys can land in the same bucket, each bucket holds its own small list of (key, value) pairs, checked directly whenever that bucket is accessed. This uses space proportional to the number of keys actually stored, not the size of the possible key range.
A fixed array of buckets, each holding a list of key-value pairs that collided into the same bucket.
Dry run for a small bucket count of 4, put(1, 10), put(5, 50)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["put(1, 10): bucket index is 1 mod 4 = 1","bucket 1 gets the pair (1, 10)","The hash function maps key 1 to bucket 1, and since bucket 1 is currently empty, the pair is simply appended"],["put(5, 50): bucket index is 5 mod 4 = 1","bucket 1 also gets the pair (5, 50), alongside (1, 10)","Keys 1 and 5 happen to share the same remainder mod 4, a collision, so both pairs coexist in the same bucket's list"],["get(5): search bucket 1's list directly for key 5","found, returns 50","The bucket the hash function points to is searched directly for a matching key, rather than scanning the whole structure"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: hash each key to a small fixed number of buckets, chaining within each bucket

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) average per operation, assuming keys spread reasonably evenly across buckets, degrading toward O(n) in the worst case if many keys collide into the same bucket.
Space: O(n), proportional to the number of keys actually stored, plus the fixed bucket array overhead.

Every operation on a key first computes the exact same bucket index via the same hash function, guaranteeing that a key inserted into a given bucket will always be searched for in that same bucket later, regardless of which operation is being performed. Chaining resolves the rare case where two different keys land in the same bucket by simply checking each pair in that bucket's short list individually, which stays fast as long as the bucket count is large enough that collisions remain infrequent.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","What happens"],"rows":[["Key not yet in its bucket's list (put)","A new key-value pair is appended to that bucket"],["Key already in its bucket's list (put)","The existing pair's value is updated in place, avoiding a duplicate entry"],["Key not found in its bucket's list (get)","-1 is returned, matching the not-present requirement"]]}

items: _hash(key) / hashKey(key) centralizes the key mod bucketCount computation in one place, so every operation, put, get, and remove, uses the exact same rule to locate a key's bucket.
put's loop checks every existing pair in the target bucket for a matching key before appending, so updating an existing key never creates a second, conflicting entry.
get's loop simply returns the moment a matching key is found in the bucket, and falls through to -1 if the loop completes without a match, directly matching the not-found requirement.
remove finds and deletes only the one matching pair from its bucket's list, leaving every other pair in that bucket, including ones that collided into it, completely untouched.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (direct addressing)","O(1) per operation","O(maximum key value)","Guaranteed O(1), but pays enormous, mostly-wasted space up front for the entire key range"],["Optimized (fixed buckets, chaining)","O(1) average per operation","O(n)","Space scales with keys actually stored; average case stays fast as long as bucketCount is reasonably chosen"]]}

blocks.text: This problem is a from scratch reconstruction of exactly how real hash maps work internally: a hash function maps keys down to a manageable number of buckets, and collisions within a bucket are resolved by simply keeping a small list, a technique called separate chaining.

items: Choosing a bucket count that is a small power of two combined with keys that share common factors, which can concentrate many keys into very few buckets and degrade performance toward the worst case.

Forgetting to check for and update an existing key within a bucket during put, instead always appending, which would create duplicate entries for the same key and make get return whichever one happens to be found first.
Removing by clearing a value to a sentinel instead of truly deleting the pair from the bucket's list, which can silently break a chaining-based implementation that expects the list itself to shrink.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Looking up a key that was never inserted","Returns -1 rather than throwing an error, since the bucket's list is simply searched and found empty of that key"],["Removing a key that does not exist","Simply does nothing, since no matching pair is found in the bucket's list to remove"]]}

items: Mention that a real production hash map also dynamically resizes its bucket array as the number of stored keys grows, to keep the average bucket size small and operations close to O(1), a refinement beyond what this exercise strictly requires.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Design a hash map, or implement a hash table from scratch" points toward two decisions: a hash function compressing keys into a small bucket range, and a collision resolution strategy, chaining being the simplest to implement correctly under time pressure.

items: How would you handle resizing the bucket array as more keys are inserted? Track the count of stored keys, and once the average chain length crosses a threshold, allocate a larger bucket array and re-insert every existing key using the new bucket count.

What if keys and values could be arbitrary objects instead of just non-negative integers? The hash function would need to be replaced with a general hashing scheme, such as combining a type's own hash code with the bucket count, while the chaining logic itself stays the same.

Could open addressing, storing colliding entries directly in other array slots instead of a separate list, be used instead of chaining? Yes, though it adds real complexity around handling removals, often requiring a special "deleted" marker, that chaining avoids naturally.

Same "compress a huge key space into a small bucket count" idea underlies every hash-based structure, from Ransom Note's frequency array to Word Pattern's mapping hash maps, just made explicit here instead of relying on a language's built-in map.
Same separate-chaining collision resolution technique used in real-world hash table implementations across virtually every programming language's standard library.
Same "trade guaranteed worst case for excellent average case" tradeoff seen whenever a hash-based structure is chosen over a guaranteed-but-wasteful direct-addressing array.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force (direct addressing): O(1) time per operation, O(maximum key value) space.
Optimized (fixed buckets with chaining): O(1) average time per operation, O(n) space proportional to actual keys stored.

items: Pattern: Hand-built hash map using a modulo hash function and separate chaining for collisions
Core Idea: Compress an enormous key range into a small, fixed number of buckets via key mod bucketCount, and resolve collisions by keeping a short list of key-value pairs per bucket
Time: O(1) average per operation
Space: O(n), proportional to the number of keys actually stored
Most Important Observation: A hash map is built from exactly two decisions, a hash function to pick a bucket and a collision strategy within that bucket, both implemented manually here
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Hash to a bucket, chain through collisions
